paragraphs: Scientific problem solving requires both reliable knowledge and good judgment about when to use external tools. The paper addresses a tension in training language models: tools can reduce hallucinations, but training models to use them can also create unnecessary dependence. Adapting while Learning, or AWL, teaches scientific knowledge alongside decisions about whether a tool is needed.

The method has two components. World Knowledge Learning trains the model on solutions generated using tools, helping it internalize scientific knowledge. Tool Usage Adaptation then separates problems into easy and hard groups according to the model’s accuracy. Training encourages direct reasoning on easy problems and tool use on hard ones, making tool selection responsive to the model’s demonstrated ability.

Across six scientific benchmarks, AWL reports 29.11% higher answer accuracy and 12.72% better tool usage accuracy than the original 8B instruction model. On four custom datasets, it also surpasses GPT-4o and Claude-3.5. These findings support training knowledge acquisition and tool selection together for the evaluated scientific tasks.
icml-2025-adapting-while-learning-ground.tldr: AWL trains language models to absorb scientific knowledge from tool-generated solutions and use tools selectively according to problem difficulty.

paragraphs: Randomized defenses aim to make adversarial attacks harder by introducing uncertainty into a neural network’s behavior. Adding noise to input data can help, but its effectiveness may depend heavily on noise settings and the dataset. It can also reduce accuracy on ordinary, unmodified inputs. This paper studies that trade-off while moving randomness into the network structure.

The proposed mechanism is stochastic deformable convolution, in which a random mask replaces the convolutional offset. By introducing randomness through this structural component, the method promotes independence from the input data and aims to generalize better across datasets. The contribution therefore concerns both where randomness enters the model and how the resulting defense is trained.

The authors analyze robust and clean accuracy through gradient cosine similarity and natural inference, then use that analysis to reformulate adversarial training. Experiments report state-of-the-art robustness and clean accuracy relative to other randomized defenses. The stated comparison supports a better balance within that family of methods, rather than establishing superiority over every possible defense.
icml-2025-adversarial-robustness-via-def.tldr: Stochastic deformable convolution introduces randomness into network structure and uses a theoretical accuracy analysis to improve adversarial defense training.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models process each token with only some of their available expert modules. A separate router usually decides which experts should participate. This paper argues that separating selection from execution can produce poor matches between tokens and experts, weakening both immediate processing and the learning of expert capabilities.

Autonomy-of-Expert replaces the router with an expert-driven selection procedure. Each expert first computes internal activations for an input, and the experts are ranked by the norms of those activations. The highest-ranking experts finish their forward passes; the others stop. The underlying idea is that activation scale reflects an expert’s capacity to handle a token, allowing the expert’s own computation to inform selection.

Evaluating every expert even partially introduces overhead, so the method uses low-rank weight factorization to reduce that cost. In language-model pretraining experiments spanning 700 million to 4 billion parameters, the approach outperforms traditional mixture-of-experts models with comparable efficiency. The results support using internal expert responses as a practical basis for allocating computation.
icml-2025-autonomy-of-experts-models-21d.tldr: Autonomy-of-Expert selects experts using their own preliminary activations, improving tested language models while retaining comparable efficiency.

paragraphs: Causal attribution asks how causes contributed to an outcome that has already been observed. Much prior work treats outcomes as binary, but many practical outcomes vary continuously. Converting these measurements into two categories can discard information or distort conclusions. This paper develops a framework for retrospective causal analysis that retains the continuous outcome and accommodates multiple correlated causes.

The authors define several posterior causal quantities, including intervention effects, total causal effects, and natural direct effects. These provide different ways to describe causal contributions after observing an outcome. The paper supplies equations showing how the quantities can be identified under sequential ignorability, monotonicity, and perfect positive rank assumptions. Those assumptions are central to the identification result.

The work also introduces an estimation procedure and establishes asymptotic properties describing its behavior as sample sizes grow. An artificial hypertension example and a real developmental toxicity dataset illustrate the approach. The contribution combines definitions, conditional identification, and estimation tools for attribution without first reducing a continuous measurement to a binary label.
icml-2025-causal-attribution-analysis-fo.tldr: The paper develops retrospective causal attribution for continuous outcomes, with identification guarantees under explicit assumptions and an accompanying estimation procedure.

paragraphs: Conformal classification returns a set of candidate labels, allowing uncertainty to be expressed through the size of that set. Coverage concerns whether the correct label is included. Existing approaches commonly build these sets using a single conformity score, which measures how well a candidate label fits. The paper investigates whether combining several scores can produce more informative sets.

The proposed method assigns weights to multiple conformity score functions and averages them. It also considers different data splitting strategies. This connects conformal prediction with model averaging: instead of committing to one scoring rule, the method optimizes a weighted combination. The objective is to reduce unnecessary labels while preserving the coverage protection that makes prediction sets useful.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis based on Vapnik–Chervonenkis theory, establishing finite-sample coverage guarantees and analyzing efficiency. Benchmark experiments report consistently smaller prediction sets than single-score methods without loss of coverage. In those evaluations, the improvement means more selective answers at the same level of protection against excluding the correct class.
icml-2025-conformity-score-averaging-for.tldr: Weighted averaging of conformity scores produces smaller classification prediction sets while preserving the paper’s finite-sample coverage guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper considers stochastic control problems with many dimensions and a finite decision horizon. A policy must choose actions despite randomness in how the system evolves. Deep reinforcement learning can address these problems, but estimating policy gradients from Monte Carlo samples often produces high variance, making the direction of improvement difficult to determine reliably.

The authors introduce Momentum Consensus-Based Optimization and Adaptive Momentum Consensus-Based Optimization. These frameworks optimize policies using Monte Carlo estimates of the value function rather than estimates of its gradients. They also include adjustable Gaussian noise to support exploration in complex, nonconvex settings. This changes the information used to guide optimization while retaining sampled evaluations of policy quality.

Numerical experiments support the approach’s accuracy and scalability across different problem dimensions. They also suggest potential extensions to mean-field control problems. On the theoretical side, the paper proves that the momentum framework can converge to an optimal policy under assumptions. The convergence claim is therefore conditional, while the broader scalability evidence comes from the reported numerical evaluations.
icml-2025-consensus-based-stochastic-opt.tldr: Two gradient-free control algorithms optimize sampled policy values, with numerical scalability evidence and a conditional convergence result for the momentum method.

paragraphs: This paper asks how far post-training can improve a small, one-step text-to-image generator without requiring image data. Diff-Instruct treats preference alignment as online reinforcement learning from human feedback. Its objective rewards outputs that score well under a human reward function while keeping the generator close to a reference diffusion process.

The central change is a score-based divergence used for regularization in place of the usual KL divergence. Although directly optimizing this objective appears intractable, the authors derive a theoretically equivalent loss whose gradient can be computed efficiently. This makes the proposed alignment objective usable for training while preserving its stated mathematical equivalence.

The resulting 2.6-billion-parameter DI-SDXL-1step generates 1024-by-1024 images in one step. On Parti prompts, it exceeds the 12-billion-parameter FLUX-dev on ImageReward, PickScore, and CLIP score while using 1.88% of its inference time. These benchmark-specific results show that suitable post-training can let a smaller one-step model outperform a larger multistep model on the measured preference-related criteria.
icml-2025-david-and-goliath-small-one-st.tldr: Score-based preference post-training lets a 2.6B one-step image generator beat FLUX-dev on three Parti benchmark scores using 1.88% of its inference time.

paragraphs: Backpropagation trains neural networks effectively, but the paper highlights three obstacles to treating it as biologically plausible: weight symmetry, dependence on global error signals, and a training process with two phases. Existing alternatives often either leave some of these obstacles unresolved or sacrifice performance. The authors seek a learning algorithm that addresses all three together.

Dendritic Localized Learning draws inspiration from the dynamics and plasticity of pyramidal neurons. Its design aims to train multilayer networks while satisfying the paper’s three biological plausibility criteria. The important comparison is therefore with learning algorithms that meet the same requirements, since high task performance alone would not establish that the biological constraints had been addressed.

The reported experiments find that DLL meets all three criteria and achieves state-of-the-art performance among qualifying algorithms. The method also generalizes across multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and recurrent networks. These findings provide empirical support for its usefulness across architectures and for pursuing biologically motivated training mechanisms without abandoning competitive performance within that constrained class.
icml-2025-dendritic-localized-learning-t.tldr: Dendritic Localized Learning meets three stated biological plausibility criteria and leads the evaluated algorithms satisfying those criteria.

paragraphs: Diffusion policies offer expressive action generation, but their usual training procedure needs samples from the desired target distribution. Online reinforcement learning cannot directly provide samples from an optimal policy that has yet to be learned. Passing policy gradients through the diffusion process is another option, but the paper identifies substantial computational cost and instability.

Reweighted Score Matching modifies the denoising score-matching loss through weighting. The proposed formulation preserves its optimal solution and low computational cost while removing the need to sample from the target distribution. It also allows training to optimize value functions. The authors derive tractable losses for policy mirror descent and maximum-entropy policy optimization, yielding DPMD and SDAC.

On MuJoCo benchmarks, the two algorithms outperform recent online diffusion-policy methods on most tasks. DPMD reports improvements exceeding 120% over soft actor-critic on Humanoid and Ant. These findings support reweighting as a practical way to connect diffusion training with online policy improvement while avoiding the expensive gradient route identified by the paper.
icml-2025-efficient-online-reinforcement.tldr: Reweighted Score Matching enables efficient online diffusion-policy training without samples from the optimal policy, producing two strong MuJoCo algorithms.

paragraphs: Reward design is a major source of human effort in reinforcement learning. Human feedback can communicate desired behavior, but collecting enough high-quality judgments is costly. ERL-VLM explores an alternative: learning reward functions from feedback generated by large vision-language models, with the aim of reducing the amount of direct human supervision needed.

The method asks a vision-language model to assign an absolute rating to each individual trajectory, meaning a sequence of agent behavior. This differs from asking which of two trajectories is better. The paper argues that individual ratings provide more expressive feedback and improve sample efficiency. It also introduces enhancements to address training instability caused by imbalanced data and noisy labels.

Experiments span both low-level and high-level control tasks. ERL-VLM significantly outperforms the evaluated methods for generating rewards with vision-language models. The results support the potential of AI-provided ratings for scalable reward learning, while the treatment of imbalance and noise highlights that obtaining ratings and learning reliably from them are both important parts of the approach.
icml-2025-enhancing-rating-based-reinfor.tldr: ERL-VLM learns rewards from vision-language-model ratings of individual trajectories and improves training stability under imbalanced, noisy feedback.

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs can supply structured facts that language models lack, but using them effectively requires accurate retrieval and efficient traversal. Graph-constrained reasoning addresses these difficulties by incorporating graph structure directly into language-model decoding. The model’s generation process is constrained to produce reasoning paths grounded in the available graph.

The key mechanism is KG-Trie, a trie-based index that encodes graph reasoning paths. It restricts decoding according to those paths, making graph structure part of how the model generates its reasoning. The framework also divides work between a lightweight model specialized for graph-constrained reasoning and a more powerful general model that performs inductive reasoning over multiple paths.

The authors report zero reasoning hallucination in this graph-grounded framework, alongside state-of-the-art results on several knowledge-graph question-answering benchmarks. They also report strong zero-shot generalization to unseen graphs without additional training. The grounding claim concerns faithfulness to the knowledge graph: the contribution is a mechanism for keeping generated reasoning tied to structured paths while still combining information across them.
icml-2025-graph-constrained-reasoning-fa.tldr: Graph-constrained reasoning restricts decoding to knowledge-graph paths and combines specialist and general models for faithful graph-based question answering.

paragraphs: Pansharpening combines a panchromatic image with a lower-resolution multispectral image to produce a high-resolution multispectral result. The task must reconstruct both spatial and spectral properties. The paper argues that treating images as uniform pixel grids limits common convolutional and Transformer models when they encounter irregular ground objects in remote-sensing imagery.

HetSSNet represents the fusion problem with a heterogeneous graph that explicitly describes relationships specific to pansharpening. Its first challenge is choosing a graph structure that captures relevant spatial and spectral relationships. A relationship-pattern generation module then extracts multiple patterns from that graph, providing several ways to represent how the image information is connected.

A relationship-pattern aggregation module combines these patterns into a unified spatial-spectral representation. It learns their importance adaptively from both local and global perspectives, allowing different relationships to contribute differently. The authors report substantial superiority and generalization in extensive experiments. The stated contribution is a complete graph-based fusion pipeline, covering relationship construction, extraction, and aggregation for the same reconstruction task.
icml-2025-hetssnet-spatial-spectral-hete.tldr: HetSSNet uses a heterogeneous graph and adaptive relationship aggregation to fuse spatial and spectral information for remote-sensing pansharpening.

paragraphs: Irregular multivariate time series contain variables observed at different sampling rates and scales. A method that treats all variables identically can miss this mismatch, even when it examines several temporal scales. Hi-Patch addresses the problem with a hierarchy of graphs that builds from individual observations toward increasingly global representations.

Each observation begins as a node. Within a patch, a graph layer captures local temporal relationships and connections between densely sampled variables. Aggregation then produces patch-level nodes. A stack of graph layers updates and combines those nodes across patches, using scale-specific networks to extract broader temporal and cross-variable features from both sparse and dense observations.

The final representation feeds task-specific decoders, allowing the same hierarchical design to support different outputs. Across eight datasets, Hi-Patch outperforms state-of-the-art models on irregular time-series forecasting and classification. These results support a multiscale approach that respects unequal sampling, with local information assembled progressively into features that span larger portions of the series.
icml-2025-hi-patch-hierarchical-patch-gn.tldr: Hi-Patch builds hierarchical observation graphs to model irregular time series across sampling rates and improve forecasting and classification.

paragraphs: Different modalities can learn at different speeds and follow different optimization directions. In joint training, this can leave one modality underused or cause modalities to interfere with each other. The paper distinguishes two goals: balanced learning across modalities and sufficient learning within each modality. Data Remixing is designed to address both through how training data are organized.

The method first decouples multimodal data and filters hard samples separately for each modality to reduce imbalance. It then reassembles data at the batch level to align gradient directions and avoid cross-modal interference. These stages target different parts of the problem: unequal learning across modalities and conflicting updates that weaken what individual modalities learn.

Experiments show that Data Remixing can be combined with existing approaches. The paper reports accuracy improvements of approximately 6.50% on CREMAD and 3.41% on Kinetic-Sounds, without expanding the training set or adding inference computation. The findings suggest that changing training-data organization can improve multimodal learning without requiring a more expensive deployed model.
icml-2025-improving-multimodal-learning-.tldr: Data Remixing reorganizes multimodal training samples and batches to improve learning balance and reduce interference without extra inference computation.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires a model to accommodate new classes while retaining what it learned earlier. Existing CLIP-based approaches often add several parameter sets and select a subset for each task. At inference time, choosing the wrong parameters for an image can damage performance. LADA changes how adaptation is organized to avoid this task-dependent selection problem.

The method attaches lightweight memory units associated with labels to a frozen CLIP image encoder. These units generate discriminative features by aggregating knowledge that is not partitioned by task. Because the adapter sits after the encoder, training does not propagate gradients into the frozen CLIP parameters, supporting efficient adaptation of the added components.

LADA also uses feature distillation for previously seen classes, protecting their representations from interference as new classes arrive. Extensive evaluations report state-of-the-art continual-learning performance. The approach combines label-specific memory, preservation of old features, and a frozen shared encoder, addressing both selection errors during inference and forgetting during successive stages of learning.
icml-2025-lada-scalable-label-specific-c.tldr: LADA adds label-specific memory after a frozen CLIP encoder and preserves earlier features to improve continual learning.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns a policy from a fixed dataset, where the quality of available experience can vary substantially between states. Uniform regularization creates a difficult compromise. Weak constraints can permit extrapolation errors and inflated value estimates, while strong constraints can make the policy mostly imitate the recorded behavior and suppress improvements from Bellman updates.

The proposed method varies regularization strength by state, adjusting how much to trust the results of Bellman-driven learning. It also applies regularization selectively to high-quality actions, aiming to avoid constraining the policy tightly around low-quality behavior. Together, these choices make the constraints sensitive to both where the agent is and which recorded actions are worth preserving.

The authors connect conservative Q-learning with explicit policy constraints, extending their approach to both value-regularized and policy-constrained offline learning. Experiments on D4RL report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in offline and offline-to-online settings. The findings support adapting constraints to the data’s uneven quality instead of imposing the same restriction everywhere.
icml-2025-learning-to-trust-bellman-upda.tldr: Selective state-adaptive regularization adjusts offline RL constraints by state and action quality, improving reported D4RL results.

paragraphs: Large batches can accelerate language-model training, but optimization quality can deteriorate as batch size grows. The paper links this deterioration to sharply increasing maximum attention logits, which create an information bottleneck in attention layers. It argues that existing trust-ratio scaling does not sufficiently control extreme query and key weights or account for their local structure.

MERIT changes how the optimizer scales updates. It uses a maximum norm to calculate trust ratios, targeting the maximum attention logit more directly. It also constructs element-wise ratios that consider local weight relationships within rows or columns. These two changes aim to make update scaling more precise and improve stability during large-batch training.

Experiments across GPT-2 model sizes report superior performance. For GPT-2 Medium trained with 48 billion tokens, MERIT supports a batch size of 6,000 without degradation relative to the standard batch size of 480. The result supports controlling extreme attention values and using finer-grained scaling as ways to preserve training quality at larger batch sizes.
icml-2025-merit-maximum-normalized-eleme.tldr: MERIT uses maximum-norm and element-wise update scaling to stabilize large-batch language-model training and preserve quality in GPT-2 experiments.

paragraphs: Meta-black-box optimization learns how to configure an optimization algorithm as it works on a task. Reinforcement learning can improve these configuration decisions across a distribution of tasks, but existing online training approaches can be inefficient. Q-Mamba learns the configuration policy from previously collected experience, aiming to retain effectiveness while reducing training cost.

The method represents dynamic algorithm configuration as a long sequence of decisions and decomposes the Q-function to simplify learning within the configuration space. Its data collection strategy balances exploration and exploitation. A decomposition-based loss incorporates conservative Q-learning to promote stable learning from the fixed dataset, linking the policy-training objective to the offline setting.

Q-Mamba also uses a Mamba architecture, combining a selective state model for long sequences with a hardware-aware parallel scan for efficient computation. Benchmarking finds performance competitive with or superior to prior online and offline baselines, alongside substantially better training efficiency than existing online baselines. The contribution joins dataset construction, value learning, and sequence modeling into one offline configuration framework.
icml-2025-meta-black-box-optimization-th.tldr: Q-Mamba learns optimizer-configuration policies from offline experience, combining decomposed Q-learning and sequence modeling to improve training efficiency.

paragraphs: Streaming generation produces output as input arrives, making the relationship between input order and output order important. Transducer models use input-synchronous decoding, which becomes difficult when a task requires non-monotonic alignments. Simultaneous translation is one such setting. This paper modifies decoding so that the model can use the history of the input stream more effectively.

MonoAttn-Transducer introduces learnable monotonic attention into the decoding process. During training, a forward-backward algorithm infers posterior probabilities for alignments between predictor states and input timestamps. These probabilities are then used to estimate context representations. This provides a way to account for alignment uncertainty without explicitly enumerating an exponentially large set of possible alignments.

The method’s significance is that access to input history helps address non-monotonic generation requirements while keeping alignment-related training tractable. Extensive experiments report that MonoAttn-Transducer handles non-monotonic alignments effectively in streaming scenarios. The stated result supports the proposed combination of history-aware decoding and efficient probabilistic alignment estimation for complex streaming generation tasks.
icml-2025-overcoming-non-monotonicity-in.tldr: MonoAttn-Transducer adds attention over input history and efficient alignment inference to handle non-monotonic streaming generation.

paragraphs: Talking-face generation must coordinate speech with a reference identity, facial expression, and head motion. Existing diffusion approaches can produce convincing videos but still struggle with lip synchronization, head posture, and detailed expression control. Playmate introduces a two-stage training framework that adds controllable facial information beyond the speech audio itself.

The first stage uses a decoupled implicit 3D representation and a motion-decoupled module to separate attributes more accurately. This stage supports expressive talking videos driven directly by audio. The second stage introduces an emotion-control module that encodes control information into the latent representation, enabling the model to generate videos with a desired emotion.

Experiments report better video quality than existing state-of-the-art methods, competitive lip synchronization, and greater flexibility in controlling emotion and head pose. These are distinct outcomes: the abstract claims a quality lead while describing synchronization as competitive. The contribution is a structured way to combine audio-driven animation with more deliberate control over how the portrayed person moves and expresses emotion.
icml-2025-playmate-flexible-control-of-p.tldr: Playmate combines a decoupled 3D representation with emotion conditioning to improve talking-face quality and control over expression and head pose.

paragraphs: Making graph neural networks more expressive often leads to deeper models or more complicated aggregation. This paper investigates whether some of that structure is redundant. It develops pruned versions of message-passing, K-Path, and K-Hop graph networks, seeking lower computational complexity while retaining useful abilities to distinguish graph structures.

The theoretical claims have different scopes. Pruning preserves the expressive power of the studied message-passing and K-Path architectures. For K-Hop message-passing networks, equivalence with the pruned version is established on regular and strongly regular graphs. The paper also shows that its pruned K-Path and K-Hop architectures have lower complexity than message-passing GNNs while offering greater expressive power.

Benchmark experiments report competitive performance with improved efficiency, supporting the practical value of removing the identified structures. The central lesson is that additional architectural machinery is not always needed to obtain stronger graph representations. The results combine formal comparisons of expressiveness with empirical efficiency, while keeping the K-Hop equivalence claim tied to the graph classes analyzed.
icml-2025-pruning-for-gnns-lower-complex.tldr: Pruning redundant GNN structures reduces complexity while preserving expressiveness in the stated settings and delivering competitive benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Text-to-image generators can distort real objects when their fixed parameters lack the necessary visual knowledge. This is especially problematic for fine-grained details and previously unseen objects. RealRAG supplements generation with retrieved real-world images, supplying visual information that the generator’s training may not have captured.

The method trains a reflective retriever through self-reflective contrastive learning. Its negative examples incorporate information about the generator’s existing knowledge, guiding retrieval toward images that compensate for what the generator is missing. The key idea is to make retrieval responsive to the generator’s knowledge gaps, so that the retrieved material contributes useful details for realistic object generation.

The framework is modular, and the authors report improvements across the types of state-of-the-art text-to-image generators they consider. One stated result is a 16.18% FID improvement for an autoregressive model on Stanford Car. These findings support retrieving real-object imagery as a way to improve realism, with the contrastive training procedure aimed specifically at selecting information that fills gaps in the generator.
icml-2025-realrag-retrieval-augmented-re.tldr: RealRAG trains a retriever to supply real-object images that fill a generator’s visual knowledge gaps and improve realistic image generation.

paragraphs: Evolutionary neural architecture search uses evolutionary algorithms to design neural networks automatically. Although many methods perform well empirically, their theoretical behavior is less developed. This paper studies expected runtime for multiclass classification, asking how long particular evolutionary search procedures take to reach an optimum in a constructed analytical setting.

The authors first introduce a benchmark and a two-level search space designed for multiclass classification and aligned with common evolutionary architecture-search settings. They then analyze (1+1)-ENAS algorithms using one-bit and bit-wise mutations. Establishing both upper and lower runtime bounds helps characterize the search effort instead of relying only on observed experimental performance.

Within the paper’s setup and notation, the reported expected-runtime bounds are O(rM ln(rM)) above and Ω(rM ln M) below for the studied mutation approaches. These results motivate considering simple one-bit mutation, despite the prevalence of more elaborate bit-wise mutation designs. Empirical studies support the theoretical analysis. The contribution is a tractable foundation for comparing mutation choices, with the runtime conclusions attached to the benchmark and search space developed.
icml-2025-runtime-analysis-of-evolutiona.tldr: The paper establishes expected-runtime bounds for evolutionary architecture search on a multiclass benchmark, supporting consideration of simple one-bit mutation.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers such as Adam retain optimizer state throughout training, adding substantial memory beyond the model itself. Plain stochastic gradient descent avoids that persistent state, but its effectiveness for language-model training is limited. SWAN investigates whether processing the current gradient can recover strong training performance while keeping the optimizer stateless.

The method combines normalization and whitening before applying SGD updates. Normalization stabilizes gradient distributions, while whitening counteracts the local curvature of the loss landscape. These operations are performed without storing optimizer state across updates. The approach therefore changes the geometry and scale of the gradient while retaining the memory footprint associated with stateless SGD.

Experiments report performance similar to Adam and a 50% reduction in total end-to-end memory. In the cited memory-efficient LLaMA training benchmark, SWAN reaches the same evaluation perplexity using half as many tokens for 350-million- and 1.3-billion-parameter models. The findings support stateless gradient preprocessing as a way to combine memory savings with effective language-model optimization in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-swan-sgd-with-normalization-an.tldr: SWAN normalizes and whitens SGD gradients without persistent optimizer state, reporting Adam-like performance with 50% lower total memory.

paragraphs: Neural solvers for partial differential equations have often operated on meshes containing at most tens of thousands of points. Industrial simulations involving complex geometries can require millions. Transolver++ targets that gap, addressing both the computational burden of larger meshes and the challenge of learning the physical information distributed across them.

The method builds on Transolver’s approach of learning physical states. It adds an optimized parallelism framework and a local adaptive mechanism for capturing those states from massive point collections. The authors report that a single GPU can accept million-point inputs and that adding GPUs permits further input growth with linear complexity. Scaling computation and representing local physical information are therefore joint parts of the design.

Experiments report a 13% relative improvement across six standard PDE benchmarks and more than 20% performance gains in million-scale industrial simulations involving car and 3D aircraft designs. Those industrial cases are 100 times larger than previous benchmarks. The findings connect greater input capacity with improved predictive performance on the evaluated engineering geometries.
icml-2025-transolver-an-accurate-neural-.tldr: Transolver++ combines parallel computation and local adaptation to solve PDEs on million-point geometries with improved reported performance.
